text:
Properly designed and maintained scrubbers can remove 99 percent of the particulate matter from stack exhausts. Therefore, only about 0.08 pounds of fly ash (about the only particulate matter in the exhausts) would be emitted for each million Btu burned from the coal and .05 pounds per million Btu's from the char. These are within the EPA standards.
A second EPA standard refers to air quality in the vicinity of the plant. The secondary standard would govern, which in effect states: The maximum quantity of particulate matter allowed near ground level on an annual basis is 
60 \text{ ug/m}^3
 (geometric mean). On a 24-hour basis, the maximum is 
150 \text{ ug/m}^3
. This standard could possibly be met by adjusting the stack height.
To determine stack height, it is advantageous to construct a mathematical dispersion model of the emissions plume through computer programming, ground level concentration for a variety of conditions can then be determined. This or other appropriate calculations will be made when the impact statement for a specific plan is prepared.

Sulfur Dioxide - The coal contains approximately 1.73 pounds of SO<sub>2</sub> per million Btu's burned. At present, the SO<sub>2</sub> is difficult to remove with scrubbers or any other pollution control device. Until current wet scrubber pilot plant studies can be consistently extended to full-scale operation, it will be necessary to assume that only 50 percent of the SO<sub>2</sub> will be removed. If the scrubbers remove 50 percent of the sulfur dioxide, the quantity leaving the stack would be 0.87 pounds per million Btu's, well within the standard.
